note.question: What determines essentially every choice involves an information collection or search phase prior to a decision-making phase that culminates in a choice?
note.overview: Essentially every choice involves an information collection or search phase prior to a decision-making phase that culminates in a choice. To study the information collection phase within an important class of search problems and understand how it influences the final choice, we embed an analytically tractable discrete choice model in a classical model of sequential search with perfect recall. Although significant progress has been made in the theory literature in analyzing consumers’ discrete choice behavior using random utility models, discrete choice through a sequential search process has not received enough attention at least in part because of analytical intractability issues.

Consideration Sets In this stream, the focus is on restricting attention to a subset of the available products by some screening pro­ cess and then making a choice within that set.
Our experimental design is broadly consistent with Berbeglia et al. (2022), who test by simulation a battery of discrete choice models (none with any search ele­ ment).

Although significant progress has been made in the theory literature in analyzing consumers’ discrete choice behavior using random utility models, discrete choice through a sequential search process has not received enough attention at least in part because of analytical intractability issues.

We build on the seminal Pandora’s Problem as a model of sequential search with perfect recall and on Exponomial Choice as a model of discrete choice (with each choice specified by a deterministic or observable utility component minus a random or unobservable utility component following an exponential distribution).

At the outset, they do not fully observe product utilities; rather, they engage in a costly sequen­ tial search with perfect recall in order to learn the idio­ syncratic utilities of various products to them.
But it can be a function of many product features and corresponding model parameters as long as they are all known by the customer.

components.explanation: In this subsection, we demonstrate the maximum likelihood estimation of our model of discrete choice via sequential search using simulated data so that we can control the ground truth, and compare it with two other models used in the literature.

components.formal: Estimation relation: In this subsection, we demonstrate the maximum likelihood estimation of our model of discrete choice via sequential search using simulated data so that we can control the ground truth, and compare it with two other models used in the literature.
conditions: At a high level, we conduct 100 iterations of data generation and model estimation, using W[EC], W[P], W[MNL], and W[PL] as the ground truth for data generation, estimating the three structural models based on training data under each ground truth, and reporting out-of-sample measures of fit.

Finally, comparing models with different distributional assumptions for the error term, while controlling the ground truth, lets us observe how the shape of the error distribution affects model performance.
Each model estimation is based on a random sample of 3,000 searches, and each out-of-sample test runs on 6,000 searches.

components.formal: Decision rule: Using the structural results presented in this subsection, we show in Online Appendix B that price optimization for a given assortment can be reduced to a search for the optimal price of the product with the highest ideal utility (p∗ 1).
conditions: Consider an assortment of n products with utility intercepts v1 > v2 >⋯ > vn.

Then, the optimal prices have the same ordering, that is, p∗ 1 ≥p∗ 2 ≥⋯≥p∗ n, and the products can be divided into three distinct groups based on their implied reservation prices, ri(p∗ i) = ui(p∗ i) γ(s,λ).
That is, the ideal utilities of the products evaluated at optimal prices must be ordered in the same fashion as the utility intercepts of the products.
Now, for any given set of utility intercepts, we know the order in which the search process must occur.
